planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun.

directions: Mariesii Variegata is a sport of the classic lacecap 'Mariesii' grown as much for its creamy white leaf margins as for its lacy blue or pink flower heads. The variegation shows best in brighter light, but some afternoon shade keeps the leaf edges from scorching in hot climates. Grow in rich, consistently moist soil and shelter from drying wind, since variegated foliage tends to be more prone to leaf burn than solid-green sports. Prune only to remove dead wood or spent flower heads right after bloom, as flower buds form on the previous year's stems.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich soil in morning sun with afternoon shade.

directions: Taube, German for 'dove,' is a lacecap hydrangea whose outer ray florets open white before aging to soft pink or rose as the flower heads mature through summer. The two-toned effect, with young and aging flowers often present together, extends the shrub's season of visual interest beyond many single-color lacecaps. It performs best in evenly moist, fertile soil with some shelter from midday sun. As with other bigleaf hydrangeas, it blooms primarily on stems formed the previous year, so avoid hard pruning in late fall or winter.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in reliably moist, fertile soil in partial shade.

directions: Geoffrey Chadbund is a free-flowering lacecap hydrangea bearing flat flower heads ringed with bright red to deep pink sterile florets around a center of small fertile blooms. It is noted for flowering heavily even on relatively young wood, making it a dependable bloomer compared with some older lacecap selections. Grow in reliably moist, fertile soil in partial shade; expect the ray-floret color to lean red to purple-red rather than blue even in acidic soil, since red-flowered cultivars respond less dramatically to soil pH than blue ones. Deadhead after flowering and limit further pruning to winter-killed wood removed in early spring.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in humus-rich, consistently moist soil in partial shade.

directions: Libelle, German for 'dragonfly,' is a white-flowered lacecap hydrangea bred for a tidy, well-branched habit and flat flower heads composed of showy sterile florets surrounding tiny fertile blooms. The white ray florets can pick up faint blue or pink tints as they age, though the shift is subtler than in mophead-type cultivars. It prefers consistently moist, humus-rich soil and some relief from the hottest afternoon sun. Because flower buds form on old wood, confine pruning to spent blooms and dead stems immediately after flowering.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in fertile, evenly moist soil in partial shade, allowing extra room for its vigorous habit.

directions: White Wave is an older lacecap cultivar valued for its large, flat flower heads edged in broad white sterile florets surrounding a dense cluster of small fertile flowers. It makes a vigorous, somewhat sprawling shrub that benefits from extra spacing compared with more compact modern lacecaps. Plant in fertile, evenly moist soil in partial shade, where the white ray florets hold their color regardless of soil pH, unlike blue or pink mophead types. Prune lightly right after flowering to shape the plant, since next year's buds set on the current season's mature wood.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Soeur Therese Hydrangea (Historic French White Mophead Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in rich, consistently moist soil in partial shade.

directions: Soeur Therese is a historic French mophead cultivar grown for its rounded clusters of pure white florets, among the earliest of the old-fashioned bigleaf hydrangeas to open each season. Its flowers stay reliably white regardless of soil acidity, since white-flowered cultivars lack the pigment that shifts color in response to soil aluminum. Grow in rich, consistently moist soil in partial shade, and mulch over winter in the cooler part of its range to protect the old-wood flower buds. Limit pruning to removing spent flower heads and winter damage shortly after the bloom period ends.
sources: Hydrangeas for American Gardens (Michael A. Dirr)

common_name: Ami Pasquier Hydrangea (Dwarf Crimson Mophead Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in partial shade.

directions: Ami Pasquier is a compact, old French mophead cultivar bearing rounded flower clusters in deep crimson-red to purple-red tones, a color range more stable across soil pH than the blues and pinks of many other mopheads. Its naturally dwarf, dense habit suits smaller borders and containers where full-size bigleaf hydrangeas would be unwieldy. Site it in humus-rich, evenly moist soil with partial shade, and avoid letting the root zone dry out during summer heat. Because it flowers on old wood, prune only to remove spent blooms and winter-damaged tips right after flowering.
sources: Hydrangeas for American Gardens (Michael A. Dirr)

common_name: Miss Belgium Hydrangea (Compact Red Mophead Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in fertile, consistently moist soil in partial shade.

directions: Miss Belgium is an older European mophead cultivar prized for its compact habit and rounded trusses of rose-red to pink florets with slightly curled, ruffled edges. Its shorter stature compared with many heirloom mopheads makes it a good fit for foundation plantings and smaller gardens. Grow in fertile, consistently moist soil in partial shade, where red and pink tones stay truer than in alkaline soils that can wash out flower color. Prune lightly after flowering to remove spent heads, since buds for next season's bloom are already set on the current wood by late summer.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in partial shade.

directions: Enziandom, German for 'gentian dome,' is a mophead hydrangea bred for tightly domed flower clusters that turn an intense gentian blue in acidic soil and shift toward purple-pink in neutral to alkaline conditions. Its dense, rounded flower form and sturdy stems help the heavy blooms stand upright through summer rain. Grow in humus-rich, evenly moist soil, and work in aluminum sulfate or elemental sulfur if a deeper blue is wanted and soil pH runs high. As with other bigleaf hydrangeas, flower buds form on the previous season's wood, so avoid cutting the plant back hard in fall or winter.
sources: Hydrangeas for American Gardens (Michael A. Dirr)

common_name: Kluis Superba Hydrangea (Deep Blue Mophead Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in fertile, evenly moist soil in partial shade.

directions: Kluis Superba is an older Dutch mophead cultivar long grown as both a florist and garden plant for its large, rounded trusses that deepen to intense blue-purple in acidic soil or rich pink-red in alkaline conditions. Its sturdy stems and heavy flower heads have made it a popular choice for cut-flower production as well as the home border. Grow in fertile, evenly moist soil in partial shade, and adjust soil pH over a season or two with aluminum sulfate or garden lime to steer flower color toward blue or pink. Prune only to remove spent flowers and winter dieback right after the bloom period, since it flowers on old wood.
sources: Hydrangeas for American Gardens (Michael A. Dirr)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade.

directions: Rotkehlchen, German for 'robin redbreast,' is a lacecap hydrangea with flat flower heads ringed in rosy red to carmine sterile florets around a center of small fertile flowers. Like other red-flowered bigleaf hydrangeas, its color is less responsive to soil pH than blue cultivars, staying closer to red or pink-red across a range of soil conditions. Grow in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade, with protection from strong afternoon sun that can fade the ray-floret color. Confine pruning to deadheading and removing winter-damaged stems soon after flowering ends, since next year's buds are already set on the current wood.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in rich, evenly moist soil in partial shade.

directions: Tokyo Delight is a Japanese-raised lacecap hydrangea noted for its large, flat flower heads with broad white sterile florets that often flush pink as they age, set against dark green foliage and red-tinted stems. It tends to flower heavily and has proven reliable in cool maritime climates, where it has long been a favorite among British growers. Plant in rich, evenly moist soil in partial shade, and mulch to conserve moisture through summer heat. Since flower buds form on the previous season's growth, limit pruning to spent flower heads and winter-damaged tips right after bloom.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in humus-rich, consistently moist soil in partial shade.

directions: Izu-no-hana, named for Japan's Izu Peninsula, is a lacecap hydrangea distinguished by double, star-shaped white sterile florets that give its flat flower heads a lacier, more intricate texture than single-floret lacecaps. The ray florets often take on faint pink or green tints as they age through the season. Grow in humus-rich, consistently moist soil in partial shade, where the fine-textured flower heads are best appreciated at close range along a path or shaded border. Prune only to remove spent flowers and dead wood just after flowering, since buds for the following year form on the current season's stems.
sources: Hydrangeas for American Gardens (Michael A. Dirr)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in humus-rich, consistently moist soil in partial shade, sheltered from drying wind.

directions: Light-O-Day is an older mophead cultivar grown chiefly for its gray-green leaves broadly edged in creamy white, a variegation pattern that stays attractive even when the plant is not in flower. Its rounded trusses of pink or blue florets, depending on soil pH, are comparatively secondary to the foliage display. Because variegated leaves are more prone to scorching than solid green ones, give it partial shade and shelter from hot, drying wind, along with consistently moist, humus-rich soil. Prune lightly after flowering to remove spent blooms, taking care not to remove the old wood that carries next year's buds.
sources: Hydrangeas for American Gardens (Michael A. Dirr)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in fertile, evenly moist soil in partial shade.

directions: Leuchtfeuer, German for 'beacon fire,' is an older mophead cultivar bred for rounded trusses of vivid red to deep pink florets that hold their intensity across a range of soil pH, unlike the blues that shift dramatically with soil acidity. Its sturdy stems help keep the heavy flower clusters upright through summer storms. Grow in fertile, evenly moist soil in partial shade, and mulch to protect shallow roots from temperature swings. Limit pruning to spent flower heads and winter-killed stems right after bloom, since flower buds are set on the previous season's wood.
sources: Hydrangeas for American Gardens (Michael A. Dirr)
